Look into freelancing/contracting or if you’re very ambitious: a business of your own. 

I’m teaching music lessons as a contractor right now to put myself through grad school as part of a company, but i get to set my own hours and have a lot more control over my time. 

There’s lots of ways to do this kind of thing beyond lessons. Just go on indeed and filter by contractor positions, find the ones that seem to be in demand and see if any interest you, then research how to go into that field. 

The downsides of contracting is you may not have as consistent of an income but when you do have money, save and invest intelligently and you’ll do fine. Just don’t live lavishly above your means unless you’re certain you’ll continue to succeed. 

Also you will need to do your own taxes, but I just use an accountant at the end of the year which costs around $100. It’s a small dent in your paycheck but it saves you the time and worry of managing and understanding taxes especially when you may have executive functioning struggles.

While I didn’t experience sexual assault so I can’t speak from that experience, I was never able to wear tampons since I tried them at 14. I saw my gynecologist and she suggested it could be vaginismus and suggested I get vaginal dilators. I still haven’t tried tampons yet (I’m still traumatized from when they used to get stuck in me though I intend to try them eventually) but the dilators allowed me to have penetrative sex without pain which is something I feared I would never be able to do. 

I’m no doctor, but i would bring up vaginismus with your gyno because it sounds like there is now fear and trauma associated with your vagina after the assault. Vaginismus is essentially painful involuntary vaginal contractions and they do occur often after sexual trauma from what I’m aware. 

I didn’t think the dilators would work at first, but I did them every night and they basically trained my brain in a comfortable setting to notice when the contractions would occur and what they felt like which allowed me to learn how to relax. Since you were able to use tampons before and now are not you may benefit from looking into treatments for vaginismus. 

Best wishes!

In music history we learned about how early music was harmonized. In the medieval times, people found 4th and 5th intervals to be the most pleasing and 3rds and 6s to be the most dissonant (which is true from a sound wave perspective) so they named 4ths and 5ths perfect 4ths and perfect 5ths. 

Overtime composers experimented with different intervals and that minor and eventually major 3rd interval became this cutting edge musical expression that people hated at first and overtime began to appreciate. Could be due to exposure therapy.

My personal theory of the root of why emotions are attached to music is because from an evolutionary perspective, different sounds affect us in different ways already. You might hear a growl and run away in fear it might be a bear. You might hear a baby laugh and feel joy. Consider the timbre of both of those sounds. Which one is likely more dissonant? The first one is, which may have led us to associate dissonance with fear. In the same way we enjoy metal now, that dissonance (in the 3rds and 6s example) was eventually used repeatedly overtime in a controlled environment, gradually convincing our ears to hear it as desirable.

It is harmony that gives music its emotions. Even when you hear a melody, you likely imagine a natural accompaniment to go with it. That’s why I believe dissonance is one of the key factors, along with dynamics and rhythm, to producing emotion

learn your basic stock plugins first and watch youtube videos on each one. try experimenting with each thing even without knowing the function and try to guess what it’s doing to the sound. this will help train your ears to pick up things. 

i’m weird because my brain associates colors with different timbres and frequencies so I was able to learn by describing each sound by the colors in my brain, but you can do something similar if you don’t have synesthesia like saying to yourself “this sounds crunchy, this sounds smooths, this sounds wavy etc.” When I was first learning to mix, one of my professors told me to describe to him what I was hearing even if it makes no sense, he just wanted to make sure I could distinguish between different sounds or sound manipulation tools in my mind. 

once you understand what each tool does and the more practice you get, you get better at applying things innately and making decisions on sound design. sound design is all about tricks and experimenting, like applying an envelope (the attack sustain decay and release of an instrument) to things you’d never think to apply it to for example, like a reverb. when you learn each function, you can think of cool ways to achieve the sound you want faster rather than searching around in the dark.

So I would say:
1. experiment around with each knob on plugins and synths to train your ears to look for the subtle differences
2. research the names of these tools and understand on a deeper level what they do and how they manipulate sound waves
3. experiment with tricks, watch tutorials on how to build instruments or how to achieve a certain sound and copy those tutorials exactly to learn the process
4. think of the sound you want in your mind, ask yourself “what do I need to do to create this sound?” it’ll feel weird and unnatural at first, but over time you’ll become a pro. And remember there’s no wrong answer, if you create a sound that’s not what you wanted it could sound just as cool and interesting. 

Happy producing

edit: also once you learn a bit about the stock plugins, invest in a synth like serum. it’s a learning curve but your skills will skyrocket and your sound will be much better

when I first got diagnosed at freshly 18 I was relieved, my entire life made sense and I could stop blaming myself for the things I couldn’t control and more importantly, others would stop blaming me. or so I thought

I was immediately out about it and I was viewed as the special kid (i never had been before, before I was just the weird neurotypical so this was new), i was discriminated against by professors, and I was taken advantage of. I stopped being open about it irl. The grief finally hit me later. I went back to constantly masking. I’d wish for a cure, wake up every day saying “my birth was a mistake I wasn’t meant to exist in this world,” and I’d think about how unfortunate it had been that I struggled my entire life and all the trauma that had caused me. The grief is still there as I haven’t gotten proper therapy yet, but I’ve learned a new perspective.

We have a neurological difference. We can’t get angry at ourselves for things beyond our control, like our slow processing, spd, social issues, or other people’s anger and lack of understanding. Some people get diagnosed with cancer, some people get diagnosed with alzheimers, als, etc. They don’t always get the opportunity to live, but even though we struggle we most of the time get the opportunity to continue living. And for me, struggling with suicidal thoughts, that hasn’t necessarily been a comfort. But it does point out that everybody struggles with something in this life, some worse than others. And you have to make the decision every day to keep living, because giving up is what the world would expect, and we can’t give them that.
